a: I will not eat it until
t: "Not eat it" or "not eat it any more"
p: Later manuscripts add "no longer": "I will not eat it any more" (KJV). The oldest lack it, which changes the sense.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott and Hort; Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi (first hand), H, Regius (L), a few others, the Old Latin manuscript a and the Coptic versions (as reported by Tischendorf); the papyrus evidence is not checked here

readings.w: A corrector of Ephraemi, Bezae, P, X, Γ, Δ, Λ, Π and most later manuscripts, most Old Latin, the Vulgate and the Curetonian Syriac (as reported by Tischendorf); Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV). Tregelles and Tischendorf printed "no longer"; Lachmann bracketed it

readings.en: I will no longer eat of it
readings.plain: I will not eat it any more until

why: The shorter reading has the stronger and older Greek support and is printed by the modern editions. "No longer" looks like a scribe's attempt to make clear that Jesus did eat this Passover and would not eat another. Tischendorf kept it, noting that similar witnesses leave "no longer" out at Mark 14:25 too, so it need not have been borrowed from there.
b: Without "no longer," the saying can be read to mean that Jesus longed to eat this Passover but would not eat it: a vow to fast until the kingdom comes. Joachim Jeremias argued for this reading. Most interpreters still think Jesus shared the meal and speaks of not eating it again; Luke's Greek allows both.

t: The longer and the shorter text of the Supper
p: Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts stop at "This is my body," leaving out the rest of 22:19 and all of 22:20. This goes with the variant at 22:20.

readings.w: SBLGNT (in brackets), NA28, Tyndale House; Papyrus 75 (about 175–225), Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi, Washington, nearly all Greek manuscripts, most early versions; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)

readings.plain: , which is being given for you. Do this to remember me.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, about 400) and the Old Latin manuscripts a, d, ff2, i and l (as reported by Metzger); in two other Old Latin manuscripts (b, e) the cup of 22:17–18 follows the bread, and the Syriac versions rearrange the verses in yet other ways
readings.en: (nothing: the verse ends "This is my body.")

why: The longer text is in almost every manuscript and version, including the very early Papyrus 75. Most scholars think the shorter text arose from a scribe's effort to remove the second cup, or from reverence that kept the full words of the rite from outsiders; Westcott and Hort, and later Bart Ehrman, argued the opposite, that the longer text was filled in from Paul (1 Corinthians 11:24–25). See the deep dive on this chapter page.
b: The words that the shorter text lacks are almost the same as Paul's in 1 Corinthians 11:24–25. That is the main argument on both sides: either a scribe copied them in from Paul, or Luke himself drew on the same liturgical tradition as Paul.

why: The evidence is divided almost evenly in age. The Plain prints the verses, as nearly all Bibles do, because they were known by about AD 150 and have been read in the church since; the brackets of the critical editions and this note mark that they may not be from Luke's own hand.
b: Added: many scholars (Westcott and Hort, Bart Ehrman and Mark Plunkett) think they were added to show that Jesus was truly human against those who said he only seemed to suffer. Removed: others (Raymond Brown, and before him many older critics) think they were cut by scribes who found a Jesus in such distress, needing an angel's help, unworthy of the Son of God. Their vocabulary and style are close to Luke's. See the deep dive on this chapter page.

why: The verse is missing from early and varied witnesses, and where it appears it stands in two different places, after 23:16 or after 23:19, which is the mark of a note added in the margin and then copied into the text at different points. Its wording is close to Mark 15:6 and Matthew 27:15. The Plain keeps the verse number, as Bibles do, and gives the added words here.

a: And Jesus kept saying, "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing."
p: This prayer is missing from Papyrus 75, Vaticanus, Bezae (first hand) and other early witnesses. It is in Sinaiticus and most manuscripts.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand and a later corrector), Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, a later corrector of Bezae, Regius (L), Ψ, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority, most Old Latin, the Vulgate, the Curetonian and later Syriac; known to Irenaeus (in Latin) and many later fathers; Textus Receptus (KJV). The SBLGNT and NA28 print it in double brackets; the Tyndale House edition prints it
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἔλεγεν· Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς, οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν τί ποιοῦσιν.
readings.en: And Jesus was saying, "Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing."
readings.plain: And Jesus kept saying, "Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing."

readings.w: Papyrus 75 (about 175–225), the first corrector of Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Bezae (first hand), Washington, Koridethi (Θ), 0124, 1241, two Old Latin manuscripts, the Sinaitic Syriac and the Sahidic Coptic (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: (the prayer is missing)

why: The Plain prints the prayer, as almost all Bibles do. Its absence from early and widespread witnesses is impressive, and Metzger's committee judged it "probably not part of the original Gospel of Luke," yet added that it "bears self-evident tokens of its dominical origin," that is, of coming from Jesus. Others, such as Nathan Eubank, argue that Luke wrote it and that scribes cut it out. Metzger's committee thought it unlikely that scribes cut the prayer out because they took the fall of Jerusalem as proof that God had not forgiven the Jews; Eubank argues for that motive.
b: Why would a scribe cut it? Some think second-century Christians, who saw the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70 as God's judgment, could not accept that Jesus had prayed for the forgiveness of those who killed him. If that is so, the omission is an early sign of hostility to Jews. Why would a scribe add it? It fits Stephen's dying prayer in Acts 7:60, which may have been the model, or it may be a true saying of Jesus that circulated by word of mouth. See the deep dive on this chapter page.

readings.en: the body of Jesus
readings.plain: the body of Jesus

why: The Plain follows NA28 and Tyndale House against the SBL edition, because the longer reading is in Papyrus 75 and nearly every other manuscript. Westcott and Hort put the words in double brackets as an addition, and the SBL edition leaves them out. "The Lord Jesus" is found nowhere else in the Gospels except the Longer Ending of Mark (Mark 16:19), but it is common in Acts (Acts 1:21; 4:33), which some take as a mark of a later hand and others as Luke's own way of naming the risen one.
b: This is the first of Luke 24's "Western non-interpolations"; see the deep dive on this chapter page.

a: He isn't here, but he has been raised.
t: "He isn't here, but he has been raised"
p: Codex Bezae and Old Latin manuscripts lack these words, a Western non-interpolation. All other witnesses have them.

why: The words are close to Mark 16:6 and Matthew 28:6, so Westcott and Hort thought they were copied in from there. But Luke's form, "not here, but raised," differs from both, and Papyrus 75 has it; most editors now print it.
b: See the deep dive on this chapter page.

a: Peter, though, got up and ran to the tomb. He bent down to peer in and saw the linen wrappings, and nothing else. Then he went off home, wondering at what had happened.
p: Codex Bezae and Old Latin manuscripts lack the whole verse. Papyrus 75 and almost all others have it.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Regius (L), Washington, Koridethi (Θ) and almost all others; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV, which adds "laid" or "lying")
readings.orig: Ὁ δὲ Πέτρος ἀναστὰς ἔδραμεν ἐπὶ τὸ μνημεῖον· καὶ παρακύψας βλέπει τὰ ὀθόνια μόνα· καὶ ἀπῆλθεν πρὸς ἑαυτὸν θαυμάζων τὸ γεγονός.
readings.en: But Peter got up and ran to the tomb; and stooping down he sees the linen cloths alone; and he went away home, wondering at what had happened.
readings.plain: Peter, though, got up and ran to the tomb. He bent down to peer in and saw the linen wrappings, and nothing else. Then he went off home, wondering at what had happened.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D) and the Old Latin manuscripts a, b, d, e, l, r1 (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: (the verse is missing)

why: The verse shares rare words with John 20:5–10, so Westcott and Hort and the RSV of 1946 treated it as an addition from John. But it is in Papyrus 75, it has features of Luke's style ("wondering at what had happened"), and 24:24 assumes that someone went to the tomb. Most editors and translations now include it.
b: If Luke wrote it, the Gospels have two independent reports of a visit by Peter to the empty tomb. See the deep dive.

a: sixty stadia
t: Sixty or a hundred and sixty stadia?
p: Codex Sinaiticus and a few others read "a hundred and sixty stadia," which fits Emmaus-Nicopolis.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Papyrus 75, Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Washington and most manuscripts; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "threescore furlongs")
readings.en: sixty stadia (about seven miles)
readings.plain: sixty stadia

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Koridethi (Θ), a few other manuscripts and some versions (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: a hundred and sixty stadia (about eighteen miles)
readings.plain: a hundred and sixty stadia

why: "Sixty" is far better attested. "A hundred and sixty" seems to have been introduced to match the distance to Emmaus-Nicopolis, the site that Eusebius and Jerome identified, though eighteen miles each way is too far for the two to walk back the same evening (24:33).
b: See the note on Emmaus at this verse.

a: as you walk?" They stopped, their faces gloomy.
t: "They stood still, looking sad" or "and are sad?"
p: The KJV makes the sadness part of Jesus' question: "as ye walk, and are sad?"

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott and Hort, Tregelles; Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, probably Alexandrinus (first hand), Regius (L, "they stopped"), the Old Latin manuscript e and the Coptic versions (as reported by Tischendorf); the papyrus evidence is not checked here
readings.en: as you walk? And they stood still, looking sad.
readings.plain: as you walk?" They stopped, their faces gloomy.

readings.w: Most later manuscripts; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: as you walk, and are sad?
readings.plain: as you walk, and why are your faces so gloomy?"

why: The difference is one verb, "they stood" against "you are." The earliest manuscripts have "they stood still," a vivid detail.

a: Our hearts were on fire inside us
p: Codex Bezae reads "Was not our heart veiled?" Other early witnesses lack "inside us."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28 (with "inside us" in brackets), Tyndale House; Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Regius (L), Washington, Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἡ καρδία ἡμῶν καιομένη ἦν ἐν ἡμῖν
readings.en: our heart was burning within us
readings.plain: Our hearts were on fire inside us

readings.w: Westcott and Hort; Papyrus 75, Codex Vaticanus, Bezae (which also has "veiled" for "burning"), the Old Latin c and e and the Sinaitic and Curetonian Syriac (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: our heart was burning
readings.plain: Our hearts were on fire

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D), which also lacks "inside us" (as reported by Metzger); some Old Latin and Coptic manuscripts have other words, such as "blinded" or "heavy"

readings.plain: Our hearts were veiled

why: "Burning" is in nearly every witness. "Veiled" may come from a scribe who thought the image of a burning heart odd, and who remembered the veil over the heart in 2 Corinthians 3:14–16.

p: The KJV names Jesus: "Jesus himself stood in the midst of them."

a: and said to them, "Peace to you."
t: "And said to them, Peace to you": a Western non-interpolation
p: The SBL edition and Codex Bezae lack the greeting. NA28 and Tyndale House include it, with Papyrus 75. A few manuscripts add "It is I; do not be afraid."

readings.w: NA28, Tyndale House; Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Regius (L), Koridethi (Θ), Ψ and almost all others; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)

readings.w: Codex Washington (W), some later manuscripts and some Latin and other versions (as reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: καὶ λέγει αὐτοῖς· Εἰρήνη ὑμῖν. ἐγώ εἰμι, μὴ φοβεῖσθε.
readings.en: and he says to them, "Peace to you. It is I; do not be afraid."
readings.plain: and said to them, "Peace to you. It is I. Do not be afraid."

why: The Plain follows NA28 and Tyndale House against the SBL edition, because the greeting is in Papyrus 75 and nearly all manuscripts. It is the same as John 20:19, which led Westcott and Hort to think it was copied from John; others answer that Luke and John share a common tradition of the appearance. The words "It is I; do not be afraid" come from the story of Jesus walking on the water (John 6:20).
b: See the deep dive on this chapter page.

t: He showed them his hands and feet (24:40)
p: Codex Bezae, Old Latin manuscripts and two Old Syriac versions lack the verse. The SBL edition prints it in brackets.

why: The verse is like John 20:20, "his hands and his side," but Luke has "feet," matching 24:39, which a copyist borrowing from John would hardly have changed. With Papyrus 75 in support, most editors print it.
b: See the deep dive on this chapter page.

a: a piece of grilled fish.
p: The KJV adds that they gave him "an honeycomb" too. The oldest manuscripts have only the fish.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Regius (L), Washington (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: a piece of broiled fish
readings.plain: a piece of grilled fish.

readings.w: Many later manuscripts; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἰχθύος ὀπτοῦ μέρος καὶ ἀπὸ μελισσίου κηρίου
readings.en: a piece of broiled fish and of a honeycomb
readings.plain: a piece of grilled fish and some honeycomb.

why: The honeycomb is absent from the early witnesses of every type. Metzger's committee thought it was added because honey had a place in early Christian rites, such as the milk and honey given to the newly baptized.

a: repentance and the forgiveness of sins
p: The editions differ. SBL and Tyndale House read "repentance and forgiveness"; NA28 reads "repentance for the forgiveness of sins."

readings.w: SBLGNT, Tyndale House; Codex Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Bezae, Washington, Koridethi (Θ) and most later manuscripts; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: repentance and forgiveness of sins
readings.plain: repentance and the forgiveness of sins

readings.w: NA28; Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and some versions (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: repentance for the forgiveness of sins
readings.plain: repentance for the forgiveness of sins

why: Both readings are early. The Plain follows the SBL and Tyndale House editions. "For the forgiveness" matches the description of John's baptism (3:3; Mark 1:4) and Acts 2:38, so scribes may have brought it in from there; or "and" may be a smoothing. The meaning hardly changes: repentance and forgiveness go together.

a: and was being carried up into heaven
t: "And was carried up into heaven": a Western non-interpolation
p: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Bezae and some Old Latin and Syriac witnesses lack these words. The SBL edition prints them in brackets.

readings.w: SBLGNT (in brackets), NA28, Tyndale House; Papyrus 75, a corrector of Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi, Regius (L), Washington and almost all others; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.en: and was carried up into heaven
readings.plain: and was being carried up into heaven

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Bezae (D), several Old Latin manuscripts and the Sinaitic Syriac (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: (the words are missing)

why: The Plain prints the words with Papyrus 75 and nearly all manuscripts. Some think scribes removed them to avoid a clash with Acts 1:3, where the ascension comes forty days later, or because the Gospel and Acts would then tell it twice; others, that they were added to make the Gospel end with the ascension. Acts 1:2 says the first book told of Jesus' deeds "until the day he was taken up," which favors their presence.
b: Without these words, Jesus simply "stepped away from them," as at Emmaus he vanished (24:31). See the deep dive on this chapter page and the note on this verse.

a: blessing God.
p: The oldest manuscripts say "blessing God," Bezae "praising God," and the KJV "praising and blessing God. Amen."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House; Papyrus 75, Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi (first hand), Regius (L), the Sinaitic Syriac and the Coptic (as reported by Metzger)
readings.en: blessing God.
readings.plain: blessing God.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D) and Old Latin manuscripts
readings.en: praising God.
readings.plain: praising God.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus, Ephraemi (corrected), Washington, Koridethi (Θ) and most later manuscripts; Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV), most adding "Amen"
readings.orig: αἰνοῦντες καὶ εὐλογοῦντες τὸν θεόν. ἀμήν.
readings.en: praising and blessing God. Amen.
readings.plain: praising and blessing God. Amen.

why: This is a textbook case of what text critics call conflation: later scribes, knowing both "blessing" and "praising," kept both. Westcott and Hort used this very verse to show how the Byzantine text grew. "Amen" was added when the Gospel was read aloud in church.
